name: Melanotan II
summary: An unapproved lab-made hormone analog injected for tanning and sometimes for sexual arousal, linked in case reports to mole changes and serious side effects.
what_it_is: Melanotan II is a synthetic peptide modeled on alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), the body's signal that tells skin cells to make pigment. Besides darkening the skin, it acts on the brain and can trigger spontaneous erections, nausea and yawning. It was tested in a few small studies between 1996 and 2000 but was never approved as a medicine. A related peptide, afamelanotide, is approved for a few medical uses.

evidence.why: Its effects on skin color and erections come from a pilot study of 3 men and a placebo-controlled crossover trial of 10 men; most safety information comes from case reports.

status_us.label: Not approved; compounding review pending
status_us.note: It is an unapproved drug; in 2007 FDA warned a seller and told consumers to stop using it. FDA took it off its Category 2 safety-risk list in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn, but it is not on the list pharmacies may compound from; an FDA advisory committee is expected to review it before the end of February 2027.

benefits.claim: Darker skin on the face and upper body in 2 of 3 healthy men in a pilot study
Erections in men with erectile dysfunction: after 12 of 19 injections versus 1 of 21 placebo injections, in a trial of 10 men
Higher sexual desire than placebo in the same 10-man trial

risks.risk: Nausea, sometimes severe, along with yawning and stretching
New or changing moles, and case reports of melanoma during or soon after use (cause not proven)
Priapism (a prolonged erection that needs emergency care), a brain condition called posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), and stimulant-like toxic reactions, in case reports
Unregulated products of uncertain content and purity; impurities may trigger immune reactions

avoid_if: History of melanoma, or many or unusual moles
Heart disease or uncontrolled high blood pressure, given reports of stimulant-like toxic reactions

before: General health check including blood pressure
during: Regular skin checks for new or changing moles
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for this unapproved drug; skin checks follow from case reports of mole changes and melanoma.

studies.title: Effect of an alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone analog on penile erection and sexual desire in men with organic erectile dysfunction
studies.finding: Erections followed 12 of 19 Melanotan II injections versus 1 of 21 placebo injections, and sexual desire rose. Nausea and yawning were more common, with severe nausea after 4 of 19 injections.

studies.title: Evaluation of melanotan-II, a superpotent cyclic melanotropic peptide in a pilot phase-I clinical study
studies.finding: Two of the three men had measurably darker skin. Spontaneous erections with yawning and stretching followed doses, and mild nausea was common.

studies.title: Risks of unregulated use of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone analogues: A review
studies.finding: Case reports link melanotan use to changes in existing moles and new atypical moles, plus four melanomas; the authors note conclusive proof of cause is lacking.

ask_your_clinician: Should I have a full skin exam, and how often should my moles be checked?
What safer options exist for the reason I am considering this, such as sun protection or treatment for low libido?
Which symptoms, such as an erection lasting hours or a severe headache, mean I need emergency care?

notes_for_editor: Seed record was out of date: Melanotan II is no longer in Category 2 (moved to FDA's 'nominated but withdrawn' list, April 2026), but it still cannot be lawfully compounded; a second advisory committee meeting is expected before end of February 2027 with no date set (sources 5, 8). Human efficacy data are tiny (3 and 10 men); the 1998 Wessells psychogenic ED study could not be opened and is omitted. Frequencies of melanoma, priapism and PRES are unknown because evidence is case reports. 'Heart disease' in avoid_if is an inference from FDA's mention of stimulant-like toxic reactions.
